analysis.one_liner: Banned racial profiling, funded police body cameras, restored voting rights after felony sentences, and cut drug sentencing disparities.
analysis.headline: Two Democratic senators introduced this criminal justice package in June 2015, and it never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made racial profiling by federal, state, and local police illegal, letting individuals sue and letting the Justice Department withhold federal grants from agencies that profile. It would have funded body cameras for police, restored the right to vote in federal elections to people not currently in prison for a felony, reduced penalties for simple drug possession, and wiped out the longer sentences for crack versus powder cocaine. It also funded job training and reentry programs for people leaving prison.
analysis.who_benefits: Black and Latino Americans disproportionately subjected to traffic stops, frisks, and searches (the bill's findings note 1 in 13 African-Americans cannot vote due to felony convictions); the roughly 5.85 million citizens barred from voting by past felony convictions; low-level drug offenders facing steep federal sentences; and communities that would have received school-truancy, crime-victim, and drug-treatment funding
analysis.who_benefits_short: People of color and formerly incarcerated citizens

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits racial profiling by any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agent, and lets individuals sue for injunctions; proof that stops in a jurisdiction have a disparate racial impact is enough to make a case [S2] [S3].
Restores the federal vote to citizens not serving a prison sentence for a felony, a right its findings say 5,850,000 Americans — including 2 million African-Americans — currently lack [S3].

Eliminates the five-times-longer federal sentences for crack versus powder cocaine and cuts penalties for simple drug possession, applying the change retroactively so already-sentenced defendants can seek reductions [S2] [S3].

Creates a $10 million matching grant program for police body cameras, with grants conditioned on community-developed use policies, data on use of force and complaints, and limits on who can view footage [S3].

Redirects 50 percent of the estimated savings from the lighter drug sentences into a fund for truancy prevention, crime-victim trauma services, and mental health and drug treatment in the courts [S3].

Authorizes $200 million a year for the Reentry Employment Opportunities program and expands Second Chance Act reentry grants, and urges federal contractors to adopt 'fair chance' hiring that delays asking about criminal records [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new grant programs; law enforcement agencies take on mandatory data collection, complaint procedures, and racial profiling policies as a condition of receiving federal justice grants; federal prosecutors lose a sentencing tool the bill's opponents in past debates defended as deterrence

drawbacks.text: The bill lets a statistical 'disparate impact' on any group serve as sufficient first evidence of profiling in a lawsuit, which police organizations have long argued pressures officers to pull back from proactive policing in high-crime minority neighborhoods — the very communities the bill aims to protect [S3].

Ending the crack-powder sentencing disparity reduces the maximum sentences available for trafficking in crack, a change some prosecutors and members of Congress have opposed on the grounds that crack markets produced more violence [S3].

Grant conditions push federal policy into state and local policing: agencies must adopt DOJ-approved anti-profiling policies, complaint procedures, and audit programs or lose Byrne and COPS funding, which small departments say is a heavy administrative burden [S3].

Body camera grants come with storage, privacy, and data-security costs that local governments must partially fund themselves through the required match, and the bill never guarantees long-term funding after the two-year grants end [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, measurable relief to people who bear the brunt of the current system: disproportionate stops and searches, lifelong voting bans, and long federal drug sentences. The costs are real but modest and mostly administrative — compliance paperwork for police agencies, some reduced penalties prosecutors would rather keep, and new grant spending. The main design risk is the disparate-impact lawsuit standard, which could produce friction with police departments; the bill tried to manage that by routing enforcement mostly through grant conditions and DOJ regulations rather than damages suits.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Cardin introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 18, 2015, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or any further action until the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 18, 2015 by Senator Ben Cardin for himself and Senator Barbara Mikulski, both Maryland Democrats, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
The full action history shows no activity after that referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — for the remaining year and a half of the Congress [S5].
The bill had only one cosponsor [S4], so it never built the bipartisan coalition that would have been needed to move criminal justice legislation through the Judiciary Committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies that would have faced profiling bans, mandatory data collection, and grant conditions kept the status quo; so did federal prosecutors who would have had to apply lighter drug sentences and retroactive reductions. No one gained anything concrete except the ability to reintroduce the idea.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats and the Republican-controlled Senate committee took no action on the bill, though the record contains no roll calls because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local)
industries.note: The bill would have conditioned federal justice grants on anti-profiling policies, complaint procedures, and stop-data reporting, and exposed agencies to profiling lawsuits — but it also offered new grants for body cameras, training, and best-practice technology. Police departments gain money while losing discretion over stops and searches.

A $10 million matching grant program to purchase or lease body cameras would have created new public-sector customers. The interest runs with the public here, since the cameras exist to document police conduct.

Lighter sentences for simple possession, retroactive sentence reductions, and reentry programs would have shrunk the population flowing into correctional facilities, reducing demand for incarceration capacity. What the industry loses, the people it holds gain.

A nonbinding provision urged the President to require federal contractors to adopt 'fair chance' hiring that delays asking about criminal records, expanding the hiring pool at little cost. The reentry employment grants also fund employer-facing job programs.
